title: Infinity
question: Can one infinity be larger than another?
objectives: Compare the sizes of two collections by pairing instead of counting
Explain why the even numbers and the fractions are no more numerous than the counting numbers
Follow the diagonal argument that the real numbers cannot be listed

key_terms.definition: Matching every member of one collection with exactly one member of another, with none left over on either side.
Able to be paired one to one with the counting numbers 1, 2, 3 and so on.
Infinite and too large to be paired with the counting numbers.
Cantor's proof that any list of real numbers leaves at least one out.

guess.prompt: Which collection is bigger: all the counting numbers 1, 2, 3, and so on, or only the even numbers 2, 4, 6, and so on?

options.text: The counting numbers, with twice as many

guess.reveal: They are the same size. Pair each counting number with its double: 1 with 2, 2 with 4, 3 with 6. Every number on each side has exactly one partner and nothing is left over.

hook: The even numbers are only half of the counting numbers, and there are exactly as many of them. Once you see why, a second surprise is waiting: some infinities really are bigger than others.

explanation.body_md:
You cannot count an infinite collection, so mathematicians compare sizes another way: by **pairing**. If every dancer has exactly one partner and nobody is left standing, there are as many dancers as partners. You never had to count them.

Apply that to infinite collections. Pair each counting number with its double.

| Counting number | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | … |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Its partner | 2 | 4 | 6 | 8 | … |

Nothing is left over on either side, so the two collections are the same size, even though one is part of the other. A collection that can be paired with the counting numbers like this is called **countable**. The fractions turn out to be countable as well.

So is every infinity the same size? No. Georg Cantor proved that the real numbers, all the points on the number line, cannot be paired with the counting numbers.

His proof imagines any list of decimals. Build a new decimal that differs from the first number in its first digit, from the second number in its second digit, and so on. The new decimal cannot be anywhere on the list. Every list misses something, so no list is complete.

The real numbers are a strictly larger infinity. They are called **uncountable**.
explanation.analogy: To check that a cinema has as many seats as people, you do not count. You ask everyone to sit. If nobody is standing and no seat is empty, the numbers match. Cantor did the same with infinite collections.
takeaways: Two collections are the same size when they can be paired with nothing left over.
The evens, the squares and the fractions are all the same size as the counting numbers.
The real numbers are a larger infinity: any list of them leaves some out.

worked_example.body_md:
Here are the first four entries of a list that someone says contains every decimal between 0 and 1.

1. 0.**3**710…
2. 0.5**6**17…
3. 0.87**5**8…
4. 0.141**5**…

Build a number that is missing.

- The first entry's first digit is 3. Choose something else, say 4.
- The second entry's second digit is 6. Choose 7.
- The third entry's third digit is 5. Choose 6.
- The fourth entry's fourth digit is 5. Choose 6.

The new number starts 0.4766… It is not entry 1, because the first digits differ. It is not entry 2, because the second digits differ. It cannot be entry 3 or 4 either, and if you keep going down the diagonal it cannot be any entry at all.

The digits above are made up, and the rule used here was to add one. Any rule that changes each digit will do, as long as you avoid 0 and 9, which can produce two spellings of the same number.

misconception.claim: Infinity is just a very large number, and all infinities are equal.
misconception.correction_md:
Infinity is not a number sitting far along the number line. It is neither even nor odd, and adding one to it changes nothing. What mathematicians measure is the size of infinite collections, and those sizes behave in their own way: a part can be as large as the whole.

Nor are all infinities equal. The counting numbers and the real numbers are both endless, yet the second collection is strictly larger than the first, and there are larger ones beyond it.

recall_items.prompt: How do mathematicians decide whether two infinite collections are the same size?
recall_items.answer: By checking whether their members can be paired one to one with nothing left over on either side.

recall_items.prompt: A collection that can be paired one to one with the counting numbers is called ___.

recall_items.explanation: The first three can each be paired with the counting numbers. The real numbers cannot.

recall_items.prompt: Hilbert's hotel is full and three new guests arrive. What instruction frees exactly three rooms?
recall_items.answer: Ask every guest to move from room n to room n + 3. Rooms 1, 2 and 3 become free.

recall_items.prompt: In the diagonal argument, why can the new number not be the 500th number on the list?
recall_items.answer: It was built to differ from the 500th number in its 500th digit.

recall_items.prompt: True or false: there are more fractions than counting numbers.
recall_items.explanation: The fractions can be laid out in a grid and walked through in diagonal stripes, which pairs them with the counting numbers.

recall_items.prompt: The even numbers and the real numbers are both infinite. What is the difference between them?
recall_items.answer: The even numbers can be paired with the counting numbers, so they are countable. The real numbers cannot be listed at all, so they are a larger, uncountable infinity.

recall_items.prompt: Why is infinity not simply a very large number?
recall_items.answer: It does not behave like a number: it is neither even nor odd, and adding to it does not make it bigger. It describes the size of an endless collection.

teach_back.prompt: Explain to a friend how there can be exactly as many even numbers as counting numbers, and then why there are more real numbers than either.

rubric.point: Sizes are compared by one-to-one pairing, not by counting.
Gives a pairing that shows a countable collection, such as each number with its double.
Describes the diagonal construction: a new number that differs from the nth entry in the nth digit.
Concludes that no list of real numbers is complete, so they form a larger infinity.

false_claims: Says the even numbers are half as many as the counting numbers
Says the diagonal argument only shows that one particular list is incomplete

challenge.prompt: Someone objects: "The diagonal argument proves nothing. When you find the missing number, just add it to the top of the list. Now the list is complete." What is wrong with the objection?
model_answer: Adding the number gives a new list, and the diagonal argument can be run again on that list to produce another missing number.
The argument does not show that one list is incomplete. It shows that every possible list is incomplete.
So no amount of patching can ever finish the job, which is exactly what uncountable means.
challenge.follow_up: Why does the same trick not show that the counting numbers themselves cannot be listed?

connections.body_md: In the 1930s Alan Turing asked whether a program could decide, for any program, whether it will ever stop. He proved it cannot, by borrowing Cantor's diagonal trick: assume a complete list of such answers exists, then build a program that differs from every entry. The limits of computing rest on an argument about infinity.

You saw that the square root of two cannot be written as a fraction. Now you can say how common such numbers are. The fractions are countable and the real numbers are not, so almost every point on the number line is irrational.

deep_dive.body_md:
**An old puzzle**

Take the square numbers: 1, 4, 9, 16 and so on. Most numbers are not squares, so there should be fewer squares than numbers. Yet every number has its own square, so there should be exactly as many. Galileo wrote about this puzzle in the 1600s and concluded that words like more and fewer simply do not apply to infinite collections.

For more than two centuries that was where things stood. Infinity was a way of saying "without end", not a thing you could reason about precisely.

**Cantor's idea: stop counting, start pairing**

In the late 1800s the German mathematician Georg Cantor found a way through. You can tell that a room has as many chairs as people without counting either, by checking that everyone sits and no chair is empty. Cantor made this the definition. Two collections have the same size if their members can be paired off, one to one, with nothing left over on either side.

For finite collections this agrees with counting. For infinite ones it gives answers that sound absurd and are not. Pair each number with its double and the even numbers match all the counting numbers. Pair each with its square and Galileo's puzzle dissolves: there are as many squares as numbers. A collection that can be paired with the counting numbers is called countable.

**The hotel that is always full**

The mathematician David Hilbert explained this with a story. A hotel has infinitely many rooms, all taken. A new guest arrives. The manager asks everyone to move up one room, and room 1 is free.

Then a bus arrives with infinitely many passengers. The manager moves the guest in each room to the room with double the number. Now every odd-numbered room is empty, and there are infinitely many of those.

Then infinitely many such buses arrive. The manager lays the passengers out in a grid, one row per bus, and walks through it in diagonal stripes, so that every passenger is reached after a finite number of steps. The same trick, applied to a grid of numerators and denominators, shows that the fractions are countable too. Between any two fractions lies another, there is no smallest one above zero, and still there are no more of them than there are counting numbers.

At this point it seems that every infinity is the same size.

**The list that cannot be made**

It is not. Cantor showed that the real numbers, all the points on the number line, cannot be paired with the counting numbers.

Suppose someone claims to have a complete list of the real numbers between 0 and 1, each written as an endless decimal. Build a new number like this. Look at the first digit of the first number and choose a different digit. Look at the second digit of the second number and choose a different one. Carry on down the diagonal.

Your new number is not the first on the list, because it differs in the first digit. It is not the second, because it differs in the second digit. It is not the millionth either. It is nowhere on the list. So the list was not complete, and since this works against any list whatever, no complete list can exist. The real numbers are uncountable: a strictly larger infinity.

**Higher and higher**

Cantor went further. Take any collection and form the collection of all its subsets. He proved that this is always strictly bigger than what you started with. Apply that to an infinite collection, then again to the result, and you climb a ladder of ever larger infinities with no top.

**A question with no answer**

Is there an infinity bigger than the counting numbers and smaller than the real numbers? The guess that there is none is called the continuum hypothesis. It has never been proved or disproved, and it has been shown to be independent of the standard starting assumptions of mathematics: they are not strong enough to settle it either way.

**How it was received**

Many mathematicians were appalled. Henri Poincaré, one of the greatest of the time, called the theory a disease. Hilbert took the other side and defended the theory as a lasting contribution. Hilbert's side won. Cantor's way of comparing sizes is now part of the foundation of mathematics.
